name: Act of July 1, 1892 restoring the north half of the Colville Reservation to the public domain
nations: Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation
promises: Not a treaty. Under the May 9, 1891 agreement the tribes were to cede the north half of the reservation in return for $1,500,000 in five instalments and the promise in Article 6 that their right to hunt and fish on unallotted ceded land would not be taken away; the agreement was to take effect only on congressional approval (Antoine v. Washington).

breaches.what: Congress declared the north half vacated and restored to the public domain and opened it to settlement, without providing the $1,500,000 the 1891 agreement promised. Congress carried the agreement into effect and authorized the payment fourteen years later, in 1906.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Act of July 1, 1892, ch. 140, 27 Stat. 62; Act of June 21, 1906, 34 Stat. 325, as described in Antoine v. Washington, 420 U.S. 194 (1975)

source.title: Antoine v. Washington, 420 U.S. 194 (1975)
source.publisher: Caselaw Access Project, Harvard Law School Library

landTaken: The north half of the reservation, Royce area 717; the Act described it as about 1,500,000 acres (see cession-1872-07-02-methow-okanagan).
compensation: The Act of June 21, 1906 authorized $1,500,000, paid in five appropriations of $300,000 from 1907 to 1911 (Antoine v. Washington). Reservation claims, including the north half, were settled in Indian Claims Commission Dockets 181-A and 181-B for $3,500,000 in 1967 (see the primary record).
today: In Antoine v. Washington (1975) the Supreme Court held that Congress, by ratifying the 1891 agreement, preserved the tribes' Article 6 hunting and fishing rights on the ceded north half against state regulation.

openQuestions: Same land and same taking as the 1892 Act breach on cession-1872-07-02-methow-okanagan, so sameEventAs points there and the taking is counted once.

treaties.json lists no present-day tribe for this row; the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation are the successors. Royce lists two areas: 717 (the ceded north half) and 718 (the diminished reservation). Not edited.

Antoine v. Washington (1975) counts the 1892 Act as the first of the statutes by which Congress approved the 1891 agreement; the primary record relies on the Indian Claims Commission's summary of the petitioners' claim that it was not ratified. The breach stands on the opening without the promised payment.
The Colville Tribes' own account of the north half was not located.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. In 1891 the Colville tribes agreed to give up the north half of their reservation for $1,500,000, keeping hunting and fishing rights there.
plain.happened: In 1892 Congress opened the north half to settlers without providing the promised payment. Congress authorized the money only in 1906, fourteen years later.
plain.today: The $1,500,000 was paid from 1907 to 1911. In 1975 the Supreme Court upheld the tribes' hunting and fishing rights on the north half.
